rv.q: This engrossing production mostly gets the measure of the trilogy.

Simon Reade’s adaptation at Southwark Playhouse captures the frenzy of late-night pub life and the thwarted longing of the central figures, but trying to squeeze so much material into little more than two hours means much of the complexity has to be jettisoned.
Affecting depiction of London lives in a vividly performed staging of Patrick Hamilton’s celebrated novels
The two-hour stage piece often falters only to be saved by blessed moments of sheer brilliance.
This is a first-class adaptation of a trilogy that speaks of today’s capital, as much as Hamilton’s Jazz Age city.

Technically, it’s striking and impressive but a fine production can’t quite compensate for the fact that, in turning three books into a fairly short play with only six actors, Reader’s adaptation sometimes feels like a symphony rescored for a sextet who can’t quite hit the right notes.

However, its considerable potential is not fully realised, with the emotional distance from its characters ultimately limiting the power of its exploration of loneliness, exploitation and human connection.
All this makes for an enjoyable, if hardly energizing, evening of Hamilitonian themes.
It’s sublimely realised in sleaze too by the predominantly youthful company led by the magisterial Maloney, fresh out of his latest Poirrot.
All brilliantly done: one of the most affordable tickets to see damn good acting and production in the capital today.

Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky, produced by Troupe, is a worthy successor to the same company's adaptation of The Forsyte Saga and serves as an engrossing introduction to the work of a largely forgotten writer.
All members of the cast of six give affecting performances, and move well in Wintour’s convincing costumes.
Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky is an excellent introduction for newbies to Patrick Hamilton who wrote evocatively about London and its dwellers, "the weird teeming aquarium of the metropolis."
The stylised writing leans heavily on subtext producing dialogue that at times appears stilted.
It’s a serviceable, if not scintillating, introduction to Hamilton’s work.
The cast play it out brilliantly, but ultimately the script is flat with no life-shaking reversals, just a simple representation of unrequited love in unsuitable relationships which would never work.
Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky is, overall, an engaging show.

Ultimately, however, the decision to condense three novels into two hours of theatre comes at the expense of character development and storytelling needed to make us care about the lives at its centre.
A gripping story, inventive staging, exceptional lighting and a young ensemble with some genuinely outstanding performances.
“Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky” is a wonderfully structured play, even if we are often thrown by its shifting and episodic nature.
It is a play which handles the emptiness of these characters, and their desperation to fill it, with some success, although ironically also finding that same sense of hollowness in itself.

cn.t: Hamilton's gritty 1920s London trilogy receives an atmospheric but uneven adaptation. Critics praise the rich period detail and strong performances, though many note the ambitious compression of three novels into two hours sacrifices psychological depth.
